title: Respiratory Infection in Immunocompromise: Broaden the Host Differential Early
bottomLine: In an immunocompromised patient, respiratory infection can progress rapidly and may involve ordinary pathogens, opportunistic organisms, drug toxicity or noninfectious lung disease. Stabilize first, define the immune defect and exposure pattern, obtain targeted microbiology/imaging early, and involve specialty/acute care sooner than for routine community infection.
recognize: Fever may be absent despite severe infection, particularly with neutropenia, corticosteroids or advanced immune suppression.
Hypoxemia, tachypnea, diffuse infiltrates, pleuritic pain, hemoptysis or new mental-status change can signal severe disease.
differentiate: Bacterial pneumonia, viral infection, Pneumocystis, fungal disease, TB, CMV, aspiration and device-related infection vary by immune defect and exposure.
Drug pneumonitis, pulmonary edema, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and malignancy can mimic infection.
assessment: Define the immune problem: neutropenia, transplant, HIV, biologic/JAK therapy, prolonged corticosteroids, chemotherapy or hematologic malignancy.
Assess oxygenation, hemodynamics, antimicrobial prophylaxis, recent hospitalization, travel/exposures and prior resistant/opportunistic organisms.
workup: Use chest imaging and syndrome-directed bacterial, viral, fungal or opportunistic testing; obtain blood/sputum cultures when they can change care without delaying treatment in instability.
Bronchoscopy or advanced sampling may be needed when noninvasive tests are nondiagnostic and the result will alter therapy.
management: Unstable, hypoxemic, neutropenic or rapidly progressive presentations require hospital-level assessment and empiric therapy matched to host risk and local protocols.
De-escalate or redirect treatment when microbiology and clinical response clarify the cause; pursue noninfectious alternatives when the expected trajectory does not occur.
medicationSafety: Renal/hepatic dysfunction and major drug interactions are common in transplant, oncology and HIV regimens; antimicrobial selection must account for them.
Do not delay indicated treatment for a perfect microbiologic diagnosis in a deteriorating high-risk host.
counselling: Teach early presentation for fever, dyspnea or oxygen decline and reinforce infection-prevention measures specific to the immune therapy/condition.
followUp: Close the loop on pending cultures/PCR/antigen studies and coordinate infectious-disease, respirology, transplant or oncology follow-up as indicated.
examTrap: Treating an immunocompromised patient with worsening hypoxemia as ordinary outpatient CAP without defining the immune defect or considering opportunistic/noninfectious causes.
oneLinePearl: In immunocompromise, the host determines the respiratory differential as much as the chest X-ray does.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society infection-screening and respiratory specialty resources
Canadian infectious-disease and oncology/transplant practice principles

title: Thoracentesis: Sample the Right Effusion and Recognize the Complication
bottomLine: Thoracentesis is a diagnostic or therapeutic procedure for selected pleural effusions, not a reflex step for every small fluid collection. Confirm a safe target, define the clinical question, use ultrasound guidance where available/appropriate, and reassess immediately for pneumothorax, bleeding or respiratory deterioration.
recognize: A new unilateral, large, symptomatic or otherwise unexplained effusion is more likely to require diagnostic sampling than a small, clearly explained stable bilateral effusion.
Therapeutic drainage can relieve dyspnea when a sizable effusion contributes materially to symptoms.
differentiate: Transudative and exudative processes have different differentials; pleural-fluid interpretation requires paired clinical/serum context.
Empyema/complicated parapneumonic effusion may require drainage beyond a one-time diagnostic tap.
assessment: Assess oxygenation, respiratory distress, anticoagulants/bleeding risk, imaging, suspected cause, effusion size/location and whether the patient can safely position for the procedure.
workup: Use ultrasound to confirm fluid location/depth and reduce wrong-site/dry-tap risk where available and within scope.
Send pleural studies matched to the question, commonly cell count/differential, protein/LDH, pH/glucose when infection is suspected, microbiology and cytology when malignancy is plausible.
management: Use trained procedural technique and appropriate monitoring; stop/reassess if the patient develops chest pain, severe cough, hypoxemia, hypotension or other concerning symptoms.
Escalate complicated infection, recurrent malignant effusion or persistent undiagnosed exudate to pleural/respirology pathways.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant/antiplatelet management is individualized to bleeding risk, urgency and local procedural policy; do not apply one universal hold interval.
Avoid blind repeated attempts when imaging does not confirm a safe pocket.
counselling: Explain the diagnostic question, expected sensations and symptoms that require immediate reporting after the procedure.
followUp: Review pleural-fluid results and ensure an unexplained exudate receives definitive follow-up rather than being lost after symptom relief.
examTrap: Ordering thoracentesis for every bilateral heart-failure effusion without asking whether the result will change management—or ignoring sudden post-procedure dyspnea.
oneLinePearl: Thoracentesis needs a question, a safe pocket and a plan for the result.
sourceBasis: Canadian pleural-procedure and respiratory specialty practice principles
Choosing Wisely Canada procedural stewardship principles

title: Pulmonary Function Tests: Pattern Before Label
bottomLine: Interpret pulmonary function testing as a physiologic pattern, not a diagnosis. Start with test quality, then identify obstruction, restriction or mixed physiology, assess bronchodilator response and lung volumes/DLCO when available, and integrate the pattern with symptoms and imaging.
recognize: Low FEV1/FVC supports airflow obstruction when interpreted against an appropriate lower limit of normal/reference framework.
Low FVC alone does not prove restriction; total lung capacity is needed to confirm restrictive physiology when full lung volumes are available.
differentiate: Asthma can have normal spirometry between episodes; COPD requires persistent airflow obstruction in the correct exposure/clinical context.
Reduced DLCO can reflect emphysema, interstitial disease, pulmonary vascular disease, anemia or other processes and is not disease-specific.
assessment: Confirm symptoms, smoking/vaping/occupational exposures, inhaler use before testing, test effort/quality and whether the study was performed during acute illness.
workup: Interpret spirometry, bronchodilator response, lung volumes and DLCO in sequence; compare prior studies when disease progression or treatment response is the question.
Use race-neutral/evidence-based contemporary reference interpretation consistent with current CTS guidance.
management: Use the physiologic pattern to refine the differential and select next testing/treatment rather than treating a single spirometry number.
Refer unexplained restriction, marked DLCO reduction, atypical obstruction or discordant symptoms to respirology as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Do not escalate chronic inhaler therapy solely from one low FEV1 without confirming the diagnosis, technique and clinical context.
redFlags: Discordant severe symptoms despite near-normal spirometry
counselling: Explain that spirometry measures airflow mechanics; it does not by itself name the disease.
followUp: Repeat testing only when it answers a clinical question such as diagnostic confirmation, meaningful treatment response or progression.
examTrap: Calling a low FVC 'restrictive lung disease' without confirming total lung capacity.
oneLinePearl: Quality first, pattern second, diagnosis third.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Pulmonary Function Testing resources, including 2023 interpretation guidance

title: Oxygen Therapy: Treat Hypoxemia, Prescribe the Target
bottomLine: Oxygen is a drug used for hypoxemia, not routine breathlessness. Define the indication, target saturation/clinical goal, delivery device, reassessment plan and chronic eligibility pathway; excessive oxygen can be harmful in selected patients with chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure.
recognize: Acute hypoxemia, respiratory distress and peri-resuscitation states may require immediate supplemental oxygen while the cause is treated.
Chronic home oxygen requires objective eligibility and reassessment rather than a one-time dyspnea complaint.
differentiate: Dyspnea with normal oxygenation needs treatment of the cause, not reflex oxygen.
COPD does not mean every patient needs a lower oxygen target; hypercapnia risk and the acute clinical context guide individualized targets.
assessment: Assess saturation quality, work of breathing, mental status, ABG/VBG when hypercapnia/acid-base status matters, baseline oxygen use, smoking/fire risk and the underlying cause of hypoxemia.
workup: Confirm chronic resting/exertional/nocturnal hypoxemia according to the relevant provincial/home-oxygen pathway and clinical syndrome.
Reassess oxygen need after stabilization because acute illness can create temporary requirements.
management: Titrate oxygen to the prescribed target while treating the underlying disease; escalate persistent hypoxemia or ventilatory failure rather than simply increasing flow indefinitely.
Home oxygen prescriptions should specify device/flow or target, timing of use and reassessment, with respiratory-service involvement where required.
medicationSafety: In patients at risk of CO2 retention, uncontrolled high-concentration oxygen can worsen hypercapnia; monitor clinical status and blood gases when indicated.
Smoking/open flame near home oxygen creates major fire/burn risk.
counselling: Teach oxygen safety, device use and that oxygen treats low blood oxygen rather than the sensation of breathlessness itself.
followUp: Reassess chronic oxygen eligibility and device needs after recovery or major clinical change.
examTrap: Giving long-term oxygen because a patient is breathless despite normal oxygenation—or increasing oxygen without recognizing hypercapnic ventilatory failure.
oneLinePearl: Prescribe oxygen with an indication, target and reassessment plan.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society COPD/home respiratory care resources

title: Lung Cancer Screening: High-Risk Asymptomatic Care Is Not Diagnostic CT
bottomLine: Lung cancer screening is for asymptomatic people at sufficiently high risk and is delivered through current provincial/territorial eligibility programs using low-dose CT. Symptoms such as hemoptysis or unexplained weight loss require a diagnostic pathway, not a screening referral.
recognize: Eligibility criteria and risk-calculator implementation vary by province/territory and can change over time.
Organized programs use low-dose CT because chest X-ray is not an effective lung-cancer screening substitute.
differentiate: Screening addresses asymptomatic risk; hemoptysis, suspicious lymphadenopathy, unexplained weight loss, metastatic features or a known nodule under surveillance require diagnostic evaluation.
Meeting referral criteria may trigger formal risk assessment rather than automatic CT eligibility.
assessment: Clarify symptoms first, then age, smoking duration/intensity, quit history, COPD, prior cancer, family history, comorbidity, willingness/fitness for potential curative treatment and current provincial coverage/program access.
workup: Use the current provincial/territorial organized screening pathway and its validated risk assessment rather than memorizing one Canada-wide age/pack-year rule.
Do not use screening LDCT to evaluate a symptomatic suspected cancer presentation.
management: Refer eligible asymptomatic high-risk patients to the organized program, support smoking cessation and ensure abnormal screening findings receive closed-loop follow-up.
Shift symptomatic patients to a timely diagnostic lung-cancer pathway.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary contrast or invasive testing before the organized pathway/radiologic assessment indicates it.
counselling: Discuss potential mortality benefit along with false positives, incidental findings, overdiagnosis and downstream procedures.
Screening does not replace smoking-cessation support.
followUp: Track completion of screening and every actionable nodule/finding until definitive resolution.
examTrap: Sending a patient with hemoptysis to a routine screening program instead of a diagnostic pathway.
oneLinePearl: Screen the high-risk patient who feels well; diagnose the patient with symptoms.
sourceBasis: Ontario Health/Cancer Care Ontario Lung Screening Program 2026

title: Occupational Lung Disease: Let the Job History Change the Differential
bottomLine: Occupational lung disease is missed when exposure history is reduced to job title. Ask what was inhaled, how much, for how long, what protection was used, whether symptoms improve away from work, and whether coworkers are affected; then match physiology/imaging to asthma, hypersensitivity, pneumoconiosis, irritant injury or malignancy risk.
recognize: Work-related asthma may improve on weekends/vacation; sensitizer-induced disease can persist after exposure stops.
Silica, asbestos, metal/wood dusts, fumes, isocyanates, organic antigens and other agents produce different syndromes.
differentiate: Occupational asthma, irritant-induced asthma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, pneumoconiosis and COPD from cumulative exposure require different workup and exposure-control strategies.
A smoker can still have occupational disease; smoking history must not erase a relevant workplace exposure.
assessment: Build a chronological job/task/exposure history including controls/PPE, spills/high-intensity events, symptom timing, coworkers, hobbies and latency.
Assess severity, oxygenation, wheeze/crackles, systemic symptoms and whether continued exposure could cause immediate harm.
workup: Use spirometry/bronchodilator testing, serial peak flow when work-related asthma is suspected, chest imaging/PFTs and specialist testing matched to the exposure syndrome.
Check safety data sheets or occupational-health resources when the agent is uncertain.
management: Reduce/remove harmful exposure when indicated, treat the respiratory condition and involve occupational medicine/respirology for complex disease or work-causation assessment.
Reporting/workplace compensation obligations vary by jurisdiction and should follow provincial/territorial rules.
medicationSafety: Medication cannot substitute for ongoing uncontrolled exposure; repeated rescue treatment while the patient returns to the same harmful environment is incomplete care.
counselling: Validate occupational concerns, document exposure carefully and explain that work modification may be part of medical treatment.
followUp: Track symptoms and lung function relative to exposure changes and ensure occupational/specialist referrals are closed-loop.
examTrap: Diagnosing smoker's COPD without asking about decades of silica/asbestos/isocyanate exposure or symptom change away from work.
oneLinePearl: For occupational lung disease, the exposure history is a diagnostic test.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society occupational/airway disease resources

title: Pulmonary Nodule: Estimate Malignancy Risk Before Choosing the Next Scan
bottomLine: An incidental pulmonary nodule is managed by malignancy probability, nodule size/morphology/growth and patient context—not by repeating CT at an arbitrary interval. Compare prior imaging first, separate screening-program findings from incidental/diagnostic nodules, and ensure every actionable nodule has an owner.
recognize: Risk rises with suspicious morphology, growth, upper-lobe location, smoking history, age and prior malignancy, but no single feature is diagnostic.
Long-term imaging stability can substantially lower malignancy concern for many solid nodules, while subsolid nodules follow different timelines.
differentiate: A nodule found in an organized lung-screening program follows that program's reporting algorithm; an incidental nodule outside screening follows the applicable incidental-nodule pathway.
Symptoms or associated mass/adenopathy can move the case from surveillance to diagnostic cancer assessment.
assessment: Review prior imaging, smoking/exposure history, prior cancer, immune status, endemic infection risk, symptoms, surgical fitness and patient preferences.
workup: Use the current radiology/program algorithm to decide surveillance CT, PET/CT, biopsy or specialty referral; avoid duplicating CT before checking for previous images.
Do not apply one surveillance interval to every nodule type.
management: Low-risk nodules may need no or interval imaging; intermediate/high-risk nodules require appropriately timed imaging, PET/biopsy or thoracic referral.
Assign responsibility for follow-up and document the due date/result pathway.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric antibiotics or corticosteroids solely to 'see if the nodule shrinks' unless there is an independent clinical indication.
counselling: Explain that most nodules are not cancer but surveillance is only safe if the follow-up actually happens.
followUp: Use a tracking system until the nodule is resolved, declared stable/no-longer-needing follow-up or transitions to definitive cancer care.
examTrap: Ordering another CT without reviewing the scan from three years ago that could already establish stability.
oneLinePearl: For nodules, prior imaging is often the highest-value test you already have.

title: Pleural Effusion: Explain the Fluid Before Treating the X-Ray
bottomLine: Pleural effusion is a manifestation, not a diagnosis. Decide whether the clinical picture already explains a likely transudative process or whether unilateral, atypical, febrile, malignant or otherwise unexplained fluid requires diagnostic sampling and further imaging.
recognize: Heart failure commonly causes bilateral effusions, whereas unilateral or markedly asymmetric fluid broadens the differential.
Pleuritic pain, fever, loculation, weight loss or recurrent unilateral effusion raises concern for infection, malignancy or other exudative disease.
differentiate: Transudates arise from systemic hydrostatic/oncotic forces; exudates arise from pleural inflammation/injury and require a different differential.
A parapneumonic effusion ranges from uncomplicated reactive fluid to complicated infection/empyema requiring drainage.
assessment: Assess dyspnea, oxygenation, fever, pleuritic pain, heart/renal/liver disease, malignancy, TB risk, PE risk, medications and prior imaging.
workup: Use chest imaging/ultrasound to characterize size and complexity; when sampled, interpret pleural protein/LDH and additional pH/glucose/microbiology/cytology according to the clinical question.
Do not sample a small, clinically typical heart-failure effusion reflexively when it is responding as expected to treatment.
management: Treat the underlying systemic cause when clear and uncomplicated.
Drain complicated parapneumonic/empyema or large symptomatic effusions according to acute/pleural pathways; recurrent malignant effusion may require definitive pleural management.
medicationSafety: Avoid repeated empiric diuretic escalation for an unexplained unilateral effusion without revisiting the diagnosis.
redFlags: Recurrent unilateral effusion with malignancy concern
counselling: Explain that pleural fluid has many causes and that testing is chosen to answer whether infection, cancer or a systemic process is responsible.
followUp: Ensure radiographic/clinical resolution or definitive diagnosis; persistent unexplained effusion requires specialty follow-up.
examTrap: Calling every pleural effusion heart failure because the patient has edema, or tapping every small bilateral effusion despite a classic responding CHF presentation.
oneLinePearl: Pleural fluid is a clue—first decide whether the cause is already clear or needs sampling.
sourceBasis: Canadian imaging and procedural stewardship resources
